articles.text: On May 25, Piedmont School District Superintendent Randy Booker informed the community that anti-Semitic messages were drawn in chalk in the area behind the high school gymnasium. “Late [May 25] afternoon, Piedmont High School Administration was alerted to the discovery of a swastika and ‘Hitler’ written in chalk on the ground,” Booker said. “As a community, we denounce this act of anti-Semitism and any messages of hate that targets a group of people based on their culture, religion, race, ethnicity, ability, gender or gender expression, or sexual orientation. These actions have no place in our schools, district, or community and stand in direct opposition to the values we share as a society.” Although the investigation is ongoing and no more information has been made public, the event occurred nine days after the City proclaimed May as Jewish American Heritage month. “In recent years, Jewish Americans have increasingly experienced anti-Semitism, including but not limited to physical attacks, vandalism, verbal and physical harassment, and hateful comments posted on social media,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King at the proclamation signing on May 16. “Piedmonters share an obligation to condemn and combat anti-Semitism wherever it exists.” The city did not respond to request for comment. articles.text: On May 25, the Piedmont Police Depar tment (PPD) announced via social media that it will increase police presence in and around all Piedmont schools. The Instagram post referenced the mass shooting of 19 children and two adults at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas on May 24 - and stated, “we cannot be too cautious.” “We have asked staff to be in the area and on campus at random times. Normally, we only enter the school campuses when called for assistance. In discussions with PUSD staff, until the end of school, you will see more [police] on campus,” PPD Capt. Chris Monahan said. The police department will discuss summer school and police presence after graduation on June 2. The effort will be conducted principally by PPD Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz. On April 16, PPD posted on Instagram that a resident had advised officers of a student who made threatening comments about bringing a gun to campus and shooting people. At the time, police officers contacted the student and parents to investigate the threat and determine the accessibility of firearms to the alleged student. On May 27, Capt. Monahan explained that the infor mation was “unfounded.” The department “determined that the student did not have the means to carry out the threats at that time,” he said. The department declined to discuss the matter further, stating that “it is a juvenile medical issue.” Statement from school district Piedmont School District Superintendent Randy Booker sent an email to the community on May 24 regarding the mass shooting. “The safety and well-being of our students and staff remain our top priority. We are fortunate to partner with the Piedmont Police Department to provide training in our schools to educate staff and students in responding to an active shooter or other internal threat,” Booker said. “I would also ask your help in reminding students of the importance that if they ‘see something,’ to ‘say something.’”

articles.text: Editor: The following letter was presented to the Piedmont School Board recently. Dear School Board: I’ll be brief because we all have a lot of emails... and some of us have kids. Piedmont teachers need to be given a raise for two primary reasons. First, teachers are humans doing incredibly valuable work who deserve to be paid a decent wage. Secondly, the Piedmont schools and School District are suffering because it is difficult to attract and retain talented, dedicated teachers because (frankly) we don’t pay wages comparable to other communities like Piedmont, such as Palo Alto, or other communities full of highly educated, well-off folks (Communities that are not particularly diverse either ethnically or economically). Looking at salaries, Piedmont School District Salaries go from around $59,480 to $107,315, according to [published salary schedules], Palo Alto teacher salaries range from $71,484 to $146,979. I love Piedmont, but if I were a new teacher, I’d go to Palo Alto given the chance, wouldn’t you? As we’re focusing on wages, looking at the numbers Palo Alto teachers make between 20% and 37% more than Piedmont teachers with comparable experience. Given this lens, a COLA of 7.5% seems inadequate and indicates we should try to do better and thereby support our kids, our community, and the high property values that depend on our excellent school system. Many thanks for your work. Christina Paul is a Wildwood School parent.

articles.text: On Tuesday May 24, 2022 at Robb Elementary school in Udalve, Texas, an 18-year-old gunman opened fire, killing 19 students and two adults as well as injuring 17 others. The shooter was killed by responding officers. This “massacre” is unacceptable. What happened was wrong and it needs to change. “Stronger gun laws” some may say. No, I say. “Walk out protests” others declare. No, I say. Ninety percent of shooters will not be affected if stronger gun laws are passed. If some sick person wants to blow up a school, some laws aren’t going to stop them. As my dad says, ”A locked door keeps honest people out”. If things are going to change we need to change as a society. On Wednesday my teacher gathered us to talk about it. Choked up, he said. “We should never start thinking something like this is normal.” We are starting to think that things like this happen and we are starting to think that it’s going to happen again and we can’t do anything. We can, but we need to do the right things. As a society we think charity is shameful and we sell lucky charms marshmallows separate from cereal (why?). The world is crazy. Let me introduce you to Salvador Rolando Ramos. He was an 18-year-old boy who was bullied and teased for his lisp. He was a loner with few friends and had a substance abusive mother. He was plagued by family dysfunction and mental health struggles. He was a high school dropout with mental health issues fascinated with guns. And then, eight days after he turned eighteen he entered a Robb elementary school with more rounds of ammo than a soldier going into battle would carry. He murdered 21 people, 19 of whom were elementary school students, injuring 17 others. This kid was messed up. He needed help – and love – all while his life literally crumbled apart. He would have been shamed for asking for help. So, let’s start with education and mental health awareness. Salvador Rolando Ramos dropped out of high school after the pandemic.

articles.text: Increase of at-home tests mean underreporting of cases New data released by the state public health agency found that new COVID reported cases per day and COVID patient-occupied beds have doubled in a month. However, the surge is far lower than what we experienced with the Delta variant spike last year. “This is nothing like the Delta spike. It is far lower and is resulting in far fewer severe cases,” explained UCSF Epidemiologist and Infectious Diseases expert Dr. George Rutherford. As we enter year three of the COVID pandemic, far more individuals are vaccinated and boosted, which may also account for cases being less severe than months prior. “Fortunately, cases remain far below what we observed during [past] surges, and hospitalizations have shown only modest increases so far,” said Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss. “A little caution can help keep it that way. If you’ve chosen not to wear a mask indoors recently, now is a good time to start masking again. Even with new variants, masks and vaccines continue to be effective in preventing the worst impacts of COVID.” The testing positivity rate, or average rate over seven days, is 7% the week of May 27 according to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH). This is a slight uptick from the week prior, where test positivity rate was reported as 6.6%. During the week of May 15 to May 21, the average time California patients waited for test results was 0.8 days. The Curative clinic at Piedmont Community Hall usually processes results for PCR tests within 24 hours. At-home COVID tests have become increasingly popular. They can be purchased at CVS Pharmacy for $20 or less, are FSA eligible, and free with most insurance plans. However, the increase in at-home testing has led to undercounting, and thereby underreporting of cases, confirmed Dr. Rutherford. “We estimate that there are probably twice as many cases occurring than are being reported through regular channels. We do, however, feel that this percentage is relatively constant over time, at least since January, so we’re fairly confident following trends in reported cases to know what’s going on,” he said.

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Pool Project has advanced to the construction documents phase. City Council approved modifications to conceptual design on May 2 along with a unanimous approval to proceed with the project. City Administrator Sara Lillevand presented a pool design package to city council members on May 2 and proposed expansions to the shallow-water activity pool. She added that the design modifications were the result of March 21 and April 4 meetings, which included a reduction in size of the recreation pool and the elimination of the majority of the second story of aquatics facility. The city council also moved forward with the proposal of an all-electric pool heating on April 4, increasing the cost of the project. (See the attached construction costs estimates, with comparison cost estimates for March 21 and March 31.) Project Architect and ELS Architecture and Urban Design CEO Clarence Mamuyac shared design development drawings and Operational Analysis Consultant Stuart Isaac discussed the implications of recommended designs made by City Council. Public testimony was received from six residents at the May 2 meeting, mostly expressing excitement for the project as well as recommendations that city council consider water polo standards when considering pool depth. City council received and considered correspondence from 15 residents before advancing the project. Some public testimony asked city council to reconsider the pool depth to serve the entire community appropriately. “I would love to have a few shallow lanes that transition into the 7-foot deep end,” said resident Heather Chan. “It is too big a leap to go from the smaller shallow pool directly into an all 7-foot deep large pool. pages.text: Wednesday, June 1, 2022 3 COVID UPDATE State releases latest data on COVID Increase of at-home tests mean underreporting of cases By Allyson Aleksey New data released by the state public health agency found that new COVID reported cases per day and COVID patient-occupied beds have doubled in a month. However, the surge is far lower than what we experienced with the Delta variant spike last year. “This is nothing like the Delta spike. It is far lower and is resulting in far fewer severe cases,” explained UCSF Epidemiologist and Infectious Diseases expert Dr. George Rutherford. As we enter year three of the COVID pandemic, far more individuals are vaccinated and boosted, which may also account for cases being less severe than months prior. “Fortunately, cases remain far below what we observed during [past] surges, and hospitalizations have shown only modest increases so far,” said Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss. “A little caution can help keep it that way. If you’ve chosen not to wear a mask indoors recently, now is a good time to start masking again. Even with new variants, masks and vaccines continue to be effective in preventing the worst impacts of COVID.” The testing positivity rate, or average rate over seven days, is 7% the week of May 27 according to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH). This is a slight uptick from the week prior, where test positivity rate was reported as 6.6%. During the week of May 15 to May 21, the average time California patients waited for test results was 0.8 days. The Curative clinic at Piedmont Community Hall usually processes results for PCR tests within 24 hours. At-home COVID tests have become increasingly popular. They can be purchased at CVS Pharmacy for $20 or less, are FSA eligible, and free with most insurance plans. City Council approved modifications to conceptual design on May 2 along with a unanimous approval to proceed with the project. City Administrator Sara Lillevand presented a pool design package to city council members on May 2 and proposed expansions to the shallow-water activity pool. She added that the design modifications were the result of March 21 and April 4 meetings, which included a reduction in size of the recreation pool and the elimination of the majority of the second story of aquatics facility. The city council also moved forward with the proposal of an all-electric pool heating on April 4, increasing the cost of the project. (See the attached construction costs estimates, with comparison cost estimates for March 21 and March 31.) Piedmont was one of the first cities in California and the first in the East Bay to issue an outright ban based upon the damage to air quality, in addition to the noise pollution created. articles.text: More than 50 years ago, KNBR disc jockeys Mike Cleary of Piedmont and Frank Dill challenged their Bay Area listeners to put on a parade, and Pleasanton was selected. It became the KNBR Good Times Parade, and anyone with a little red wagon could enter. A Mariners group at the Pleasanton Presbyterian Church entered with a Viking ship the first year, then came up with the idea of the tubby sailors carrying mops. The group quickly became a comic marching group. Though many of the men were veterans of various branches of the military, there was a belief that slavish obedience to commands was counterproductive, so the Balloon Platoon was born. Invitations soon came to participate in other communities’ parades. In 20 years, the group has trooped in several bowl games, appeared at the Indianapolis 500, marched in the Christmas parade in London. Though not bearing bagpipes, the Platoon went to Edinborough Photo by Ken DeCrosta The Balloon Platoon, based in Pleasanton, has been a staple of the Piedmont 4th of July Parade for more than 12 years. in 2000 to participate in the Millennium Pipe Festival. One spring the Balloon Platoon appeared in the National Cherry Blossom Festival parade in Washington, D.C. The group meets rarely, only to decide which parade invites to accept. “We usually reject offers that are strict forward motion parades,” explained leader Hal Strunk. “The Marine Corps band does that really well – we do not.” The age of Platoon members ranges from 21 to 80 and all are associated with the church in Pleasanton. As the Balloon Platoon passes by today, look for its special routines: Shake-n-Bake, pirouettes, carousels, big pinwheels, the Manual of Mops, and a 21 Mop Salute.
articles.title: “Look at those funny men, Mommy.”

articles.text: The Barrelhouse Jazz Band has been playing traditional (Dixieland) jazz in the Bay Area since 1972. Like the earliest traditions of jazz music, the Barrelhouse boys sprang from a church. More than 48 years ago a small group of musicians at the Montclair Presbyterian Church formed a traditional jazz band. The band’s focus remains the West Coast brand of New Orleans-style jazz developed by San Francisco musician Lu Watters using a two-trumpet sound. The band loves to see people dancing to its music, something that brings out the best in the Barrelhouse musicians. The band often plays for church services in several denominations in the Bay Area, providing joy among the parishioners. In addition to playing swing music and fox-trots for dance music, the band plays struts, stomps, blues and rags. Band members are director Al Flood (clarinet & sax), Chuck McLain (trombone & vocals), pianist Margaret McElwain, Jim Lockie-Brown on banjo, Viki Jacobsen (bass sax), and Art Wood and Joel Jacobsen on trumpet. Photo by Ken DeCrosta With Greg Bloom driving, the Barrelhouse Jazz Band rolls down Highland Avenue in last year’s Piedmont 4th of July parade.

articles.text: Here comes the summer, a time when adults and children alike want to have outdoor fun. Engaging in play is an important part of early childhood and contributes to healthy brain development - the benefits are cognitive, physical, social, and emotional. Honestly, it’s good for people of all ages. For children, it helps with language, communication, and emotion control. For adults, play reduces stress, and improves brain functionality. And playing together – a departure from the structured segmentation of the pandemic home/office/gym/classroom/playground space where we do separate things next to one another – enhances learning and creativity benefits for both. According to Richard Louv, author of The Last Child in the Woods, playing outside, due to its relatively unstructured nature, also has the added benefit of feeding creativity and imagination. When children spend time playing outside the opportunities to invent, discover, pretend, and problem-solve are bountiful. Dragon fun at Children’s Fairyland This kind of break allows children (and adults) to attend to structured participation and formal zoom-room in a much more effective way. Working at Children’s Fairyland, I have had the benefit of looking out my magical window to see children become swashbuckling mates on a pirate ship, play peekaboo with a donkey, climb on the back of the happy dragon, or catch bubbles blown by an elf. I also see their adults running behind them full of glee, smiles, relief, and with a cup of coffee. Ever yone deser ves this moment to explore, imagine, create, play, scream, and run. Invest in restorative self-care for the whole family – get outside and play! Kymberly Miller is Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, America’s first storybook theme park, located on the shores of Lake Merritt in the heart of Oakland since 1950.

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation’s Board of Directors approved a $3,350,000 grant to Piedmont schools for the next school year, 2022-23, based upon its fundraising this past year through the Giving Campaign. The grant focuses primarily on teacher retention with 72% of grant funds supporting teacher salaries, inclusive of librarians and other specialists. Another 20% invests in student support staff, such as paraeducators, classroom aides, and counselors, and 8% for classroom support, curriculum development, diversity, equity and inclusion work, and professional development. After salary support, professional development opportunities for teachers and staff are a key recruitment and retention tool, leading to a significant increase in funds for this line item. Based on input from surveys, the grants committee recommended that the additional funding be used to continue two newer programs whose government funding was ending. PEF funds will maintain the expanded tutoring program and extended mental health counseling in the district. PEF will fund two elementary school priorities: aides to re-open school libraries at lunchtime for student use, and the continued use of paraeducators to supervise lunchtime at each school. The middle and high school representatives prioritized a secondary reading specialist, who will provide ongoing support for older readers. “This year’s process was really special since the Giving Campaign raised far more money than expected,” says PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. “We were able to satisfy PUSD budget needs and save some programming.” Piedmont parent clubs sent out surveys which generated nearly 500 people offering views on the current distribution of funds, and their priorities for additional fund expenditures. Survey results are available at: Piedmontedfoundation.org/ o u r-i m p a c t / 2 0 2 2 -f u n d i n gsurvey/. The grants were recommended by the year’s PEF Grants Committee, which included the presidents of each parent club, several parent support groups, and PEF board members.

articles.text: Sports, games & crafts offered to middle school students Lucas Scherman, son of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman, returns for the second year to lead Scherman Summer Camp. Campers will learn new games, get fresh air, practice new skills, make friends and be themselves. Campers will have fun playing kickball, double-dutch, capture the flag, poker, dominos, and more. Lucas, aided by brothers Julian, 19, and Quincy, 15, will teach the art of wood-burning and how to make paracord survival bracelets. Scherman Summer Camp is a screen-free, good old-fashioned camp. The camp is open to students entering grades 6-9, and will be held at Wildwood School lower playground. One-week sessions begin the week of July 11 and continue for nine weeks. Morning classes run from 10:00 a.m.-1:00 p.m., and afternoon sessions are from 2:00-5:00 p.m. To register and for more information, call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 420-3070 or visit: Register. capturepoint.com/reg/cat_program_class_detail.cfm?s=&t=&- season_id=24069&program_ id=1420272&family_mbr_str=.

articles.text: Little learners can unleash their curiosity and imagination in the newly created OMCA Kids: Nature Playspace at Oakland Museum of California. The area is designed for the unique needs of children ages 2 to 5, along with their families and caregivers. The Playspace, located within the Gallery of California Natural Sciences, opens June 4 to the public, with a preview of OMCA members on June 3. Play is critical to every child’s healthy development and the Nature Playspace offers something for everyone – from building materials and nature-themed puzzles to hands-on activities that spark creativity, wonder, and joy. The youngest museum visitors can discover the animals that reside in Oakland’s streams, hills, and backyards. The Playspace gives families a fun, safe place to play, and to build community with other families. The Oakland Museum of California is located at 1000 Oak Street, Oakland. Call 318-8427 or go to Museumca.org for advance ticketing. Museum hours: Wednesday – Sunday – 11:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. Friday – 11:00 a.m.–9:00 p.m. The new “Kids: Nature Playspace” at OMCA opens on June 4.

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School teacher Anne Smith invited the Post into her Period 4 Yearbook class on May 13 to view their work as writers, editors and creators of a news broadcast called The PMS Front Page. Now in their second year, the news team produces two, eight-minute videos per week on Wednesdays and Fridays, with the help of the middle school IT guru Adam Saville. The broadcast looks like a regular nightly news show, using a green screen for the news anchors appearing to be at a real TV news desk. Samantha Huy n h, who worked on the yearbook last year, explained the genesis of the project. “This year, coming back to school we wanted to make sure that we all get to see what happens at school and the benefits of it, so we started this broadcast idea,” she said. Quincy Antaya films the anchors of the middle school front page, Ava Rivera (left) and Sadie Shoop. The class takes place in room 125, the former woodshop class that now serves as a home base for ceramics, yearbook, a computer class, a fabrication lab, and for the video broadcast. A closet in the classroom was painted green for the green screen, and camera equipment was purchased with donations from families. The news crew on the record- 8th grade yearbook editors Bodie Ironside (left), Skylar Best, Sparrow Lieu, and Samantha Huynh, display the result of their work. ing side of the studio consists of two anchors, a teleprompter operator, and a camera person. The production side includes a audio engineer working on a sound board, and a director with a walkie talkie connected to the anchors. Two producers stitch it together on a tricaster to make the transition between segments. “Last year we produced one or two videos. This year we have a huge technical setup with a whole team dedicated to making broadcasts, with a weekly schedule, a joke segment and various features,” said Bodie Ironside, who serves as director. “I’m really impressed with how it has grown.” The entire class participates in the production, as students cycle through the various roles during the year. Student reporters and camera people conduct interviews on and off campus for segments ahead of time, and the producers transition the footage into the live recording. “It is really cool to be using Madden Yeung (left) operates a sound board next to Piedmont Middle School yearbook teacher Anne Smith, Sparrow Lieu, Andrew Bouris, video director Bodie Ironside, and producers Hadley Hayes and Adrian Kondakova (right). Anchors Sparrow Lieu (left) and Stephanie Lee deliver a Quote of the Day from B.B. King: “The beautiful thing about learning is that no one can take it away from you.” professional equipment that actual news broadcasters use. I have also learned a lot of communication skills. articles.text: Piedmont Makers awarded husband and wife Helen Potter & John Lambert the 2022 Maker of the Year award at a year-end barbecue celebration on Monday, May 30. Helen and John have been on a six-year journey with Robotics in Piedmont with their sons Charlie and Henry. They were part of the founding team for the FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) Piedmont Pioneers in 2016, the second Piedmont robotics team after Scotbotics. They created a great experience for that founding team, and with that energy created incredible momentum behind robotics in Piedmont. That soon expanded to FIRST LEGO League and FIRST Robotics Competition. Three years ago, Helen and John decided to take on their next challenge and formed the Highlander FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team. They contributed their energy, knowledge and inspiration to make it happen. They contributed their garage and turned it into Piedmont’s unofficial Fab Lab with high-end digital equipment like a CNC router and laser cutter. They basically operated the team out of their home for the first 2-1/2 years, but they knew the team needed a permanent home. They catalyzed a fundraising campaign with Piedmont Makers that ultimately resulted in raising $420,000 for the high school’s Engineering Lab, now John Lambert and Helen Potter were named winners of the 2022 Maker of the Year Award by the Piedmont Makers. the permanent home for the Highlanders in the STEAM Building. This FRC season was a culmination of that energy as the team advanced to the semifinals of the Sacramento Regional, the quarterfinals of the Silicon Valley Regional, and ultimately the semifinals at the World Championship. They also welcomed a “third child,” the Highlander robot Selkie. Both of their sons took many lessons from their robotics team and have chosen to study engineering in college - Henry at Worcester Polytechnic Institute in Worcester, Massachusetts, and Charlie at Harvey Mudd College in Claremont, California in the fall. Seven years after founding the Pioneers, the community of Piedmont now has more than 50 robotics teams with 400 students in grades K-12. Not incidentally, John Lambert is now working for the school district as Manager of the Engineering Lab. “Because of all of this, the Piedmont Makers board could not be more pleased to award Helen Potter and John Lambert our 2022 Makers of the Year award,” announced David Ragones, president of Piedmont Makers.
articles.title: Helen Potter, John Lambert receive Maker of the Year Award

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School 6th graders renewed a decades-long tradition on Friday, May 27 by participating in the popular Greek Olympic games at Witter Field. The event serves as an end-of-school year celebration, coupled with a culmination of their studies of Ancient Greece. Students were divided up into four city-states – Athens, Sparta, Olympia, and Rhodes – and competed for top awards for the winning city-state. Rhodes was declared the overall winner with the most overall wins. The events included tug-ofwar, jump rope. long jump, a 3-legged race, shot put (softball), discus (frisbee), javelin (toilet plunger), and relay races. Citystates also competed against each other musically by reciting their city-state’s anthem and designing individualized jerseys. “I definitely loved how hard all the teachers and parent volunteers worked to make it all come together,” said 6th grader Samantha Pell. Student Olympians rotated through each event with faculty members and parents helping record the athletic feats. “All in all, the kids have been doing great and having fun, and Students competed for their city-states of Athens, Sparta, Olympia, and Rhodes. that’s the whole point. There have been some rough landings in the long jump sand pit, so I expect some of their spinal columns to be feeling that tomorrow morning,” said parent Xenia Meyer who was recording the long jump results. The students’ athletic prowess may only be rivaled by their historical knowledge. This reporter did not have to go too far to find students eager to share their observations of their favorite Greek gods and goddesses. “I really like Hades, the brother of Zeus and the god of the underworld,” explained Avi Tug-of-war is a student favorite event every year at the Greek Olympics. Colt Hitchcock sticks a long jump landing. The relay races garnered stiff competition and unorthodox rules as students were asked to skip, hop and strafe as well as sprint. Boguslavsky. “Zeus’s daughter Persephony ate a single pomegranate seed from the underworld and could not come back, so she became Hades’ wife and has to remain in the underworld for onethird of the year.” While Rhodes tallied the most victories, the Greek Olympics of 2022 will be fondly remembered by all participants as a grand return to tradition after a twoyear absence, with friendly competition and teamwork, things that have been hard to come by in the last couple of years. articles.text: Piedmont native Mackie McDonald competed in another Grand Slam last week, advancing to the third round of the prestigious French Open before losing to No. 11 Jannik Sinner of Italy in three sets on Saturday, May 28. To get there, McDonald upset No. 22 seed Nikoloz Basilashvii of Georgia in three sets on Thursday, May 26 and defeated Italy’s Franco Agamenone in four sets in the opening round on Monday, May 23. Following the tournament, McDonald’s ATP Tour world ranking jumped nine positions to No. 51, two spots shy of matching his career high ranking of No. 49. In the opening round, Mackie defeated Adamenone after dropping the first set, 1-6, 6-2, 6-3, 7-6 (7-3). McDonald was great on the return, claiming seven of eight break points and 45 points as the receiver, while also winning 74 points when serving despite having just one ace on the day. McDonald’s second-round win came against Basilashvii, the No. 26 player in the world in three sets in dominant fashion by scores of 6-3, 6-1, 6-4. McDonald gained seven break points out of 25 opportunities, which showed his prowess in challenging as the returner. Basilashvii struggled while serving with six double faults compared to Mackie’s one. McDonald’s third-round loss in three sets (6-3, 7-6 (8-6), 6-3) was against Sinner, an Italian player ranked No. 12 in the world. Sinner won with help of four aces and won 75 percent of the time on his first serves. McDonald also competed in the doubles ladder in the French Open with Tommy Paul. They defeated Aisam-ul-Haq Qureshi and Aleksandr Nedovyesov in the first round on May 25, 3-6, 6-2, 6-3. In the second round the American duo defeated No. 10 seeded Bruno Soares of Brazil and England’s Jamie Murray, 7-6 (9-7), 4-6, 6-3. McDonald and Paul lost in the third round to No. 6 seed Neal Skupski of England and Dutchman Wesley Koolhof in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2. McDonald will now prepare for his next Grand Slam tournament later this month at the Wimbledon June 27-July 10 in London. Stay tuned for more coverage of McDonald’s matches this summer. articles.text: Bouquets to Art, the de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser and annual display of artwork-inspired floral installations, will begin on June 7. Now in its 38th year, the event is back to full-capacity following a virtual event in 2020 and a hybrid, limited-capacity event last year. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. It is presented by the volunteer members of the Fine Arts Museums, and has generated $7 million since its inception. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Visitors will be greeted with a large-scale aerial artwork piece by Bay Area artist Windy Chien. Entitled The Three Dragons, the hand-knotted artwork hangs in the museum’s Wilsey Court. Those who visit during the week of Bouquets to Art will have a chance to view Hung Liu’s large piece Resident Alien, first exhibited at the Capp Street Project in 1988 and exhibited by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco last year. The painting, arguably Liu’s most famous, depicts her own “Green Card” on a larger-than-life scale. It is now in the collection of the San Jose Museum of Art. “Hung Liu is uniquely positioned to tell the stories of immigrants to the United States. In 2020, she celebrated the milestone of having lived an equal number of years in China and the United States. As one of the foremost painters in the United States, Liu is a testament to the fact that our brightest citizens are often born under foreign skies,” said Janna Keegan, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art and Programming at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Bouquets to Art is a weeklong event that officially begins on Monday evening, June 6, with the traditional opening-night party. Between June 7 and June 12, a series of book launches, speaker events, and raffles will take place. For a full list of programming, visit https://www.famsf.org/ press-room/bouquets-art. Tickets sold out weeks prior to the event in 2021. Reserve yours now by visiting https://deyoung. famsf.org/bouquets-to-art. Bouquets to Art begins next week. Fresh new look, no guesswork! articles.text: This is the last weekend to see “Memento: Jayashree Chakravarty and Lam Tung Pang” at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. The exhibition, part of an ongoing series of singular exhibitions at the museum entitled Today’s Asian Voices, ends on Monday, June 6. The exhibition marks the inaugural Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery installation, Memento, which includes two contemporary works that speak to global issues of urbanization and political uncertainty. The Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery is formerly used for special exhibitions and has recently been transformed into a dedicated space for a rotating selection of both modern and contemporary works. Viewers will see Personal Space by Chakravarty (2001), an 8-foot-tall, 30-foot-wide work built from painted strips of paper. An immersive video by Hong Kong-based mixed media artist Pang entitled A day of two Suns (2019), combines unsynchronized images from four projectors that combine with the shadows of museum visitors and moving objects. “This work is prophetic and nostalgic,” said Head of Contemporary Art Abby Chen about the newly acquired work. “It documents a city, and a system, in the process of fading and awakening.” For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/memento-jayashreechakravarty-and-lam-tung-pang/. Asian Art Museum is located at 200 Larkin Street in San Francisco. (415) 581-3500.

He ventured to Chicago at the suggestion of Muddy Waters to look for a record label and began a long, successful business relationship with producer Leonard Chess, who ran jazz clubs on the South Side of Chicago. Chuck Berry borrowed heavily from white people’s genres. Maybellene, his first hit, was a remake of the 1938 Bob Wills’ country hit Ida Red. Maybellene was named after a bottle of mascara by Leonard Chess in the studio. Contrary to the usual swing rhythm used in electric guitar roots genres like blues, R&B and swing in the forties, Chuck Berry used straight rhythm in all his hits: Maybellene, Roll Over Beethoven, Rock and Roll Music and Johnny B. articles.text: There were two big programs at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last weekend. The first was a piano program by Eric Tran. The second was a return engagement of the San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra. Eric Tran grew up in Piedmont, and I don’t think we’ve had a greater treasure. His artistry was acknowledged at an early age. The muses and Apollo have been with him ever since. I think he is pursuing his PhD at the University of Wisconsin, but PhD or not, he deserves the title Maestro. His recital in Piedmont on Saturday gave ample proof of his accomplishments. Owing to a previous engagement, I missed the first half of the program. I arrived in time to hear him take us on a picturesque trip to the Austrian concert side. One of Beethoven’s most original compositions is his Sixth Symphony which is known as the “Pastoral”. Most of us know it in the original version for orchestra. But Franz Liszt arranged it for solo piano. In this version it loses absolutely nothing. It is a work of genius in itself. Eric plays with a composer’s understanding of music. The multihued pastoral symphony proved a perfect vehicle for his broad talent. All of us know the original version… And a work of genius it is! But Liszt appropriates that very genius and transforms it into a grand symphony for the piano. When Tran plays it, no one will miss the orchestra. How impressive is that?! Everything that he does is done with a casual charm. The sonorities rise from the piano in an effortless fashion. Because of this, the listeners can appreciate the music all the more. Mandolins in Piedmont The concert on Sunday afternoon was a completely different sensibility. The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra returned to the Piedmont Center for the Arts after the hiatus due to the pandemic. A brief word of explanation is due. The mandolin is a userfriendly version of the violin. It has the same tuning as the violin but uses a guitar-like pic instead of the bow to make the tone. Mandolins can play all the music that the violin plays, but with less effort…and the results are very good. The conductor/music Director of SF Mandolin Orchestra is the Achille Bocus, founder and leader of San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra. Italian born Achille Bocus. He is both an inspiration and a man of many parts. While the Mandolin is his main instrument, he is also a professional bass player, a composer and arranger as well as an outstanding conductor. Bocus arranged all of the compositions that the orchestra performs. His conducting is crystal clear. You could watch him conduct with the sound turned off and know exactly how to play. That’s the way conducting should be. Because of this, the mandolin orchestra plays above their abilities. They also take their time, and in doing so, they make an expressive presence simply because there is no haste. All of these things result in a performance of uncommon sensitivity. Especially notable is to understand that these are not professional musicians. An occasional clinker here or there was compensated for by lofty music making. Of special mention was Bocus’ performance of Schubert’s magnificent “Arpeggione Sonata.” The brief program notes offered a good insight into what we heard: “Music can bring us to an enchanted world. All you need to do is open your imagination and fly to joyful meditation.“ The caveat… Anyone who has attended performances at the Piedmont Center of the Arts or attended an art show knows what marvelous things are going on. When things are going well, it is a good idea to let them alone. Advice like this has stood humanity in good stead for a long time. Unfortunately, some of the folks in City Hall have other ideas. The PCA has been successful Piedmont native, pianist and composer Eric Tran.

The subtext of the film that is never explored is the question as to whether people, in mental and physical extremis, who are so lost can ever truly be salvaged, no matter the sincerity and commitment of the salvager. The film offers a stark glimpse of the more than 11,000 homeless people living in L.A., confined mainly to 50 blocks referred to as Skid Row. It’s as if every lost, broken soul has been carried there by a tide of poverty, mental illness, drug abuse, many tormented by a panoply of demons, now wandering the Darwinian streets trying only to survive another day. What Lopez does offer Ayers is the hand of friendship, discovering that there are moments when that is enough. But there are also moments, lots of them, when it isn’t. Because there is only the most fragile bond connecting Lopez and Ayers, the film seems strangely remote. Ultimately for Ayers, there is no redemptive moment. For Lopez there is no breakthrough, when the two men face one another in a flash of lucidity and understanding. In truth, Ayers has fled into a world apart and chooses to remain there. His only consistent bridge to others and to himself is music, his lifeline – except when it isn’t. The Soloist. Directed by Joe Wright. Starring Jamie Foxx, Robert Downey, Catherine Keener and Tom Hollander. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2009. Now Streaming on Prime/ VUDU. Lights Out, released in 2016, is an effective, compact horror-thriller that uses a minimalist conceit – fear of the dark – to its full advantage. I would judge that there is not a horror film made today that can avoid the criticism that it is derivative; and so the challenge becomes how to make the familiar sufficiently original to be downright creepy. Lights Out manages to do that in spades. Just the title signals that when the light on the nightstand or the one in the ceiling begins to flicker, bad things are going to happen. Here’s the set up for this tidy little chiller: A specter – called Diana – has returned to inhabit a spooky old house and torment an emotionally fragile single mom, Sophie (Maria Bello), and her increasingly terrified, sleep-deprived 10-year-old son, Martin (Gabriel Bateman). Martin wakes and hears his mother having late night conversations with someone/something in the dark of her bedroom. Finally, desperately, he turns to his estranged sister, Rebecca (Teresa Palmer), for help. She has long ago left the family and lives a kind of Goth, hip life over a tattoo parlor. Her boyfriend is perpetually kept at arm’s length, implying some attachment or childhood abandonment issues that are tangentially explored. Diana, who vanishes when the lights go on and appears when the lights go off, is a long-limbed, snake silhouette whose mission is the elimination of all all who are close to Sophie. They were childhood friends, stemming from a time when the two were committed to a mental institution for depression. It was there Diana died during treatment. Now this malevolent apparition has returned to take possession of Sophie’s life. Sophie is the catalyst, and Bello perfectly balances the sincere jeopardy she feels for herself and her family and her wacko delusions, foremost being that she and Diana are “friends.” Ultimately it’s her family that is in harm’s way, not Sophie. And it’s Rebecca and Martin who are subjected to the murderous machinations of Diana. They quickly discover that light is essential if they are to Gabriel Bateman and Teresa Palmer star in Lights Out. survive. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Lilo and Stitch. Lilo and Stitch is a Disney animated feature, released in 2002, and nominated for an Oscar at the 75th Awards ceremony. It was hand-drawn with a rich palette of lush, vivid colors. It’s family friendly, poignant, and at times even beguiling and will bring to mind the extraordinary film E.T., long overdue to be discovered by a new generation of kids. At the center of the story, set on the Hawaiian island of Kauai, are Lilo (Daveigh Chase), a 7-year-old Hawaiian girl, and her older teen sister Nani (Tia Carrera). They recently lost their parents in a car accident, and are now orphaned. Lilo, always rambunctious, is now struggling to cope with her loss. She is lonely, ostracized from her hula class, and troubled at school. Nani, feeling a bit desperate, takes her to an animal shelter where they pick out a “dog,” which is a small blue koala-like critter that she names Stitch. In reality Stitch is an escaped E.T. from a world faraway. He’s actually an experiment called 620, and created to cause a world of chaos. Though Lilo and Nani have a strong sister bond despite their arguments, their social worker, Cobra Bubbles (Ving Rhanes), doubts that Nani can care for Lilo alone. He thinks Lilo is too quirky, feeds peanut butter to the fish and takes strange pictures of beachgoers, and has strange-looking dolls. Meanwhile, since Stitch has escaped from his home planet, two representatives, mad scientist Dr. Jumba Jookiba (David Ogden Stiers), 620’s creator, and agent Wendell Pleakley (Kevin McDonald) of the Galactic Federation, are sent to earth to look for him. Though Stitch was created to cause chaos and bedevilment, Lilo and the diminutive E.T fashion a strong bond, and with Nani form a small nuclear family, referred to in Hawaiian as O’hana. Gradually the idea of O’hana comes to be the center of the story. Lilo introduces Stitch to Elvis albums, hula dancing, and surfing with Nani. Meanwhile the two Federation E.T.s are in the hunt for Stitch. Lilo and Stich is filled with gags and energy and intergalactic conflict. Kids will enjoy the characters in a story that ends with an action-packed aerial chase. Lilo and Stitch. Directed by Dean DeBlois & Christopher Sanders, Walt Disney animation. With voices of Daveigh Chase, Tia Carrera, Christopher Sanders. 1 hr., 25 min, Rated PG. Released in 2002, Now streaming on Disney+/ VUDU/Prime.

articles.text: Part 45 of an ongoing biweekly series. Just before the pandemic in 2019, I spent a month walking the Camino de Santiago in northern Spain. This is the most wonderful place I have seen anywhere for walkers. For those unfamiliar with the Camino, it is a popular pilgrimage started in the middle ages. People from all over the world walk this route for spiritual reflection, to admire the cultural heritage and beauty of the country, or simply for the exercise and pleasure of walking. There are actually numerous routes of the Camino de Santiago (The Way of St. James, as example) starting in different countries in Europe, all winding hundreds of kilometers, and all ending up at the main cathedral in the city of Santiago de Compostela in northwest Spain. Like most people who make this trek, after arriving at the Camino, I didn’t get onto a train or bus or into a car for a month, but covered 267 kilometers, The pedestrian trails take many forms over the length of the Camino, from dirt paths in the country, to paved paths in the villages, to passages over historical Roman bridges. walking from place to place along a marked route that passes through countryside, along various roads, through wonderful small villages and some larger cities. Walkers stay in different types of numerous accommodations, have their meals, and drink coffee in the many locally owned establishments along the way. I found it an incredible journey, both introspective and fun. The only reservations I made were for my first and last nights in Spain. Considered a prime example of the more recently named “slow tourism” movement, it represents a choice of experience and meaningful reflection, instead of trying to squeeze in too much in as little time as possible—a perfect fit for the walking experience. What I think is especially relevant about this place for us in Piedmont, is the remarkable accommodation of the pedestrian in virtually all the small towns, villages and larger cities that walkers encounter along the way. There are many places to stop and rest along streets where pedestrians clearly have the right of way. And in the medium sized, and (somewhat) larger sized cities through which this Camino passes, you experience carefully thought out pedestrian car-free zones that have become natural municipal plazas and gathering places used by both visitors and locals. The final destination of all the Camino routes is the Praza Obradoiro in front of the Catedral in Santiago de Compostela. Not a very large city, with around 96,000 population, its urban design is highly influenced by accommodation of the incredible number of pedestrians who arrive here on foot and experience the place strictly as pedestrians.

articles.text: Piedmont to try self-haul program this summer The City of Piedmont is planning a program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to pick up from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday and will close for the season in the fall. The compost is firstcome, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee availability of compost. To pick up compost, residents should bring a shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials. Pickup trucks must have a tarp on their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected by Republic Services in communities participating in curbside organics collection services. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with soil aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses and that it be composted. More information can be found on the City’s news and notifications page. If questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov or (510) 420-3058.

articles.text: The Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) will be on board NASA’s Artemis 1, the 2023 trip to the moon, NASA’s first since 1972. The public got its first look at a full-scale replica of NASA’s water-hunting Moon rover last weekend at Chabot Space & Science Center in the Oakland hills. pages.text: Wednesday, June 1, 2022 23 your Oakland Zoo Bison ready to return to the wild of Montana On May 26, The Oakland Zoo returned 13 American Bison from their herd to the wild of Montana to join their historic lineage as part of the Zoo’s Bison Restoration Project in partnership with the Blackfeet Nation. This marks the second transfer of bison to restore free-roaming bison to Blackfeet land and nearby Yellowstone National Park. “We’re very happy to be working with Oakland Zoo. It is so important to return this iconic animal and its historic bloodline to our culture and preserve that culture for generations to come. For centuries, the buffalo have taken care of us. It is now our turn to take care of them,” said Ervin Carlson, President of the Intertribal Buffalo Council, Blackfeet Nation. The returning group – four mothers, seven two-year-olds, and two one-year-old calves – are all descendants of the iconic ‘Pablo Allard’ herd. Free compost program for residents Piedmont to try self-haul program this summer By Alyssa Dykman The City of Piedmont is planning a program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to pick up from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday and will close for the season in the fall. The compost is firstcome, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee availability of compost. To pick up compost, residents should bring a shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials. Pickup trucks must have a tarp on their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected by Republic Services in communities participating in curbside organics collection services. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with soil aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses and that it be composted. More information can be found on the City’s news and notifications page. If questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov or (510) 420-3058. articles.text: A generous offer from Nancy and Dave DeRoche provided the opportunity for the Walking on Wednesdays group to have a second tour of the legacy of architect Albert Farr in Piedmont. Nancy and Dave shared that Farr was the owner of their Oakland Avenue house for 25 years in the early 20th Century. He didn’t design it, but made major modifications. One week earlier, Will Adams, a planner, urban designer, architect, and Post feature writer, led a tour of some of Farr’s most famous buildings in Piedmont, including City Hall, and Piedmont Community Church. Dave DeRoche has collected ancient artwork from Africa, Oceania, and the Americas for decades, so the group knew his house would be special. Will Adams was available to come back, so this also provided the opportunity to see more Farr-designed homes before visiting the DeRoche house. A large turnout of 37 people and two K-9 best friends showed up at the Exedra on a lovely Wednesday morning, May 25. As the group assembled, another offer from Dave and Nancy was shared with the group. Their upper Oakland Avenue portion of Piedmont, which continues up to Blair and Scenic Avenues, was a bit of bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Will Adams writes the biweekly “Walking Piedmont” feature in the Post in which he observes “the built environment of a beautiful city.” In his remarks at the start of the day’s walk, Will complimented the Wednesday Walking group as being a model for community walking. It was now time to two Albert Far-designed homes, one on Crocker Avenue and another nearby on Lincoln Avenue that Farr designed for the same owner. On the way, the walkers were able to revisit the recently sold mansion at Wildwood and Sheridan Avenue, one of Farr’s masterpieces. The group continued to Crocker to a house just off to the right at wildwood and Crocker, referring to research done by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi, Farr designed this house for Henry Drew Nichols. He was born in 1874 in New York and moved to Oakland in 1890. In June 1900, he married Ethel Kellogg, the granddaughter of Hiram Tubbs who founded the Tubbs Cordage Company in San Francisco, a business that started during the Gold Rush and was the first to manufacture rope west of New England. In 1905, Nichols contracted Farr and builder Charles Stockholm to build the two-story frame house on the east side of Crocker Avenue. The cost of construction was $11,370, and Henry and Ethel moved in just two months before the San Francisco earthquake in April 1906. Will Adams explained that Farr designed this Craftsman house high on the lot to provide views of San Francisco Bay from the West-facing rooms. It is a six bedroom, four and a half bath, and 7,818 square foot home. Large curved bays in the living room and dining room provided expansive views of the Bay in 1905. Nichols lived in the house until 1922 when he again hired Farr to build a second home around the corner on Lincoln. The walkers continued up to the second Farr house on Lincoln. It wraps around to Crocker, where there is a driveway leading to a gate with a garage, and the back of the house. The front of the house is on Lincoln, and the entrance is less visible with an ivy-covered wall and columns providing privacy. It is the childhood home of Saturday Night Live cast member Chloe Fineman, a 2006 graduate of Piedmont High School. It was now time to visit the DeRoche house, where Nancy said the house was built in 1897 for a member of Frank C. Havens’ family. She and Dave led the group past Pre-Columbian Aztec and Mayan art objects into the house. A set of stairs with a 19th Century feel to them took the walkers to the living area where there are countless museum-quality pieces of Tribal Art, some 2,000 years old, and one estimated at 3.000 years old. Many of them were burial pieces from Africa, as well as Central and South America. At the back of the house, Nancy had beverages, cakes, and other refreshments ready for the group to enjoy, The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The first time I made these “foolproof” biscuits, I followed the original recipe for Strawberry Drop Biscuits from New York Times Cooking. They were a winner and I’ve kept the recipe for repeat versions. Jerrelle Guy’s recipe encourages switching up the fruit, using other berries or diced stone fruits. Now that we’re edging toward summer fruits, this is a perfect time to get this easy baking project into your rotation. These biscuits are just a hint sweet and perfect for breakfast, brunch, or afternoon tea. You could split them crosswise for a very fruity berry shortcake too. Blueberry Drop Biscuits Adapted from Jerrelle Guy, New York Times Cooking Makes 6 biscuits, each about 4” round INGREDIENTS • 1-1/2 cups all-purpose flour • 1/4 cup granulated sugar • 4 teaspoons baking powder • 1/8 teaspoon sea salt • 1/2 teaspoon finely grated lemon zest, just the outermost yellow part, optional • 6 tablespoons cold butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes • 2/3 cup whole blueberries • 1/2 cup icy cold water • 1/4 cup heavy cream plus additional 1 tablespoon to brush on top • Turbinado sugar, or other coarse grind sugar to sprinkle on top INSTRUCTIONS 1. Place an oven rack in the center of the oven. Preheat oven to 425° F. Line a large baking sheet pan with parchment. Set aside 2. Whisk the flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, salt, and lemon zest in a large mixing bowl. Toss the pieces of butter into the flour mixture to coat. Using your fingers or a pastry cutter, work the butter into the flour until the mixture is mealy and small pieces of pea-size butter remain. (I prefer using my fingers for more control and tactile satisfaction. But if your fingers are warm, you may have to use a tool to prevent the butter getting too soft.) 3. Add the blueberries and toss with a fork to combine. Make a well in the center of the mixture and add the 1/2 cup ice cold water and 1/4 cup heavy cream. Continue tossing with the fork until the dough is just evenly damp and shaggy. Be careful to not overwork the dough too much. Add more water if needed, 1 teaspoon at a time, if the dough is too dry to work with. (It will be shaggy, with some dry bits, but needs to hold together enough to retain its shape when forming the dough into biscuits.) 4. Drop six mounds of dough onto the baking sheet, spacing at least 1-1/2 inches apart. This will be about 1/2 cup each of dough. Pat and shape the dough into as round a shape as the dough allows, firmly patting any stray bits of dough into place. 5. Lightly brush the tops with 1 tablespoon of heavy cream and sprinkle with turbinado sugar, or any other coarse sugar crystals. 6. Bake until deep golden brown and cooked through – about 15 minutes. Remove from the oven and transfer the biscuits to a wire rack to cool for about 5 minutes. 7. Serve warm or at room temperature. NOTE: The baked biscuits will freeze well. To serve, thaw and reheat in a 350°F oven for about 5 minutes. Take care to not overdo the reheating to avoid over-dry biscuits. articles.text: Judith Swope Clark, 49-year resident of Piedmont, died May 27, 2022 of Lewy Body dementia complications at her home in Piedmont. She was 76. Born on July 26, 1945 in Howard Memorial Hospital in Willits, California, she was the daughter of Glenn Swope and Anita Hoffman. Her parents divorced in the early 1950s, a very difficult event for Judie, and they both continued to live most of the rest of their lives in Willits. Her father, a CHP officer, died in 1995, and her mother died in 2010. Except for a brief detour with her mother and sister to Oakland during her parents’ breakup, Judie grew up in Willits alongside Tom Clark in the same class. The precocious Judie skipped 8th grade and stepped ahead to high school. Judie and Tom began dating in 1962 when they were 15. They married in 1968 in Berkeley. In 1973, shortly after Tom began practicing law, Judie and Tom purchased a house in Piedmont, where they have lived ever since. Judie was noteworthy for her fast mind, sharp wit, reading abilities, artistic sensibilities, organization skills, gentleness, love for animals and children, compassion for the disadvantaged, and completing daily New York Times crossword puzzles in ink. She graduated from Willits High School in 1962 and in 1966 received a B.S. degree in Anthropology from the University of California, Berkeley. For a brief period she taught school in Oakland. After helping put Tom through law school by working at UC Berkeley in various administrative capacities, Judie graduated from Golden Gate Law School in 1977 and began practicing law at the Oakland law firm where she clerked while attending law school. He legal career ended their daughter Olivia was born in 1978. Judie devoted much of her adult life to caring for her daughter and helping her overcome serious medical problems, including seizures resulting from removal of a brain tumor in 1984. Judie was a very active quilter, designing and making quilts, often in her house, with two separate groups of other Piedmont mothers. She was also active for many years in Junior Alliance that supported Lincoln Child Center in Oakland and Piedmany hours and overnight visits with Tom and Judie until his mother, Melanie, suddenly died at age 40 In 2012 Judie was diagnosed with Lewy Body dementia and gradually lost her ability to speak, stand or walk. Eventually, Tom hired caregivers to help Judie in their home. In 2018 Tom added to their house a new downstairs bedroom, bathroom and kitchen extension, and installed a chairlift from the sidewalk up the 52 steps to their house. Tom’s goal always was to keep Judie at home with him and a team of caregivers, no matter how her condition might worsen, and to ensure that Judie’s life would be as good as he could make it. Judie picked out their Piedmont house, loved it dearly and took the lead responsibility for a major renovation to the house in 1988. During their 61 years together, Judie was a faithful, honest and loving friend, as well as wife to Tom for 54 years. Tom has lost the best friend in his life. He will be eternally grateful that Judie civilized him, treated him so well despite his shortcomings and devoted her life to caring for their daughter Olivia. During her final years, Judie received excellent care from her several caregivers, Tina Smith, Ovetta and Shaniesa Gill, Nikki Howell, Nanettee Cansceco and Eden Wildemichael. Oakland Kaiser Permanente staff, especially nurse Dee Dee Bellong, provided wonderful in-home hospice care during the final weeks of her life. Judie was beloved by Tom’s entire family. She was close to Dave Sinclair, her brother-in-law, and Warren Jorgensen, both Willits classmates. She was particularly grateful for her enduring lifelong friendship with LeAnna Spence, a classmate from Willits. In addition Judie cherished her close friendship with Tom’s cousin James Curtiss and her sister-in-law Joan’s friend Peggy Cash. Judie is survived by her husband Tom; her daughter Olivia of Pleasant Hill; her niece Sandhya Clark Singh (Steven) of Teaneck, New Jersey; her sister Jayne of Los Angeles; Jayne’s children Troy Brown (Mary) of San Pablo and Shari Brown of Santa Rosa. She is additionally survived by many friends and an extended family. Judie Clarke, a Piedmont resident for nearly 50 years, passed away on May 27. She was 76. mont’s Dress Best for Less that supported the Piedmont Education Foundation Additionally, Judie was also very involved with her mother’s family winery in Napa Valley. Her maternal grandmother Rose was one of 12 children of late- 1800s Swiss emigrants Anton and Caterina Nichelini who homesteaded and founded the still-operating Nichelini winery in Chiles Valley in the eastern hills of Napa Valley. Judie was instrumental in the formation of the Nichelini Family Corporation that gathered the fractional interests of Anton and Caterina’s far-flung progeny. For many years Judie served as Secretary of the Nichelini Family Corporation, and was always partial to her great uncle Fred Nichelini, the founding President of the corporation. Tom was a self-taught winemaker. Judie and Tom, together with Tom’s sister Joan and her husband Dave Sinclair, and Tom’s brother Hugh, purchased property in 1982 in Sonoma County near Calistoga. Over the next 33 years, operating under the name Petrified Forest Vineyards, they maintained rental property, planted a vineyard from which they made 22 annual vintages of wine, and constructed a cabin retreat. pages.text: Wednesday, June 1, 2022 25 Obituary Longtime Piedmont resident Judie Clark dies May 27 Judith Swope Clark, 49-year resident of Piedmont, died May 27, 2022 of Lewy Body dementia complications at her home in Piedmont. She was 76. Born on July 26, 1945 in Howard Memorial Hospital in Willits, California, she was the daughter of Glenn Swope and Anita Hoffman. Her parents divorced in the early 1950s, a very difficult event for Judie, and they both continued to live most of the rest of their lives in Willits. Her father, a CHP officer, died in 1995, and her mother died in 2010. Except for a brief detour with her mother and sister to Oakland during her parents’ breakup, Judie grew up in Willits alongside Tom Clark in the same class. The precocious Judie skipped 8th grade and stepped ahead to high school. Judie and Tom began dating in 1962 when they were 15. They married in 1968 in Berkeley. In 1973, shortly after Tom began practicing law, Judie and Tom purchased a house in Piedmont, where they have lived ever since. Judie was noteworthy for her fast mind, sharp wit, reading abilities, artistic sensibilities, organization skills, gentleness, love for animals and children, compassion for the disadvantaged, and completing daily New York Times crossword puzzles in ink. She graduated from Willits High School in 1962 and in 1966 received a B.S. degree in Anthropology from the University of California, Berkeley. For a brief period she taught school in Oakland. After helping put Tom through law school by working at UC Berkeley in various administrative capacities, Judie graduated from Golden Gate Law School in 1977 and began practicing law at the Oakland law firm where she clerked while attending law school. He legal career ended their daughter Olivia was born in 1978. Judie devoted much of her adult life to caring for her daughter and helping her overcome serious medical problems, including seizures resulting from removal of a brain tumor in 1984. Judie was a very active quilter, designing and making quilts, often in her house, with two separate groups of other Piedmont mothers. She was also active for many years in Junior Alliance that supported Lincoln Child Center in Oakland and Piedmany hours and overnight visits with Tom and Judie until his mother, Melanie, suddenly died at age 40 In 2012 Judie was diagnosed with Lewy Body dementia and gradually lost her ability to speak, stand or walk. Eventually, Tom hired caregivers to help Judie in their home. In 2018 Tom added to their house a new downstairs bedroom, bathroom and kitchen extension, and installed a chairlift from the sidewalk up the 52 steps to their house. Tom’s goal always was to keep Judie at home with him and a team of caregivers, no matter how her condition might worsen, and to ensure that Judie’s life would be as good as he could make it. Judie picked out their Piedmont house, loved it dearly and took the lead responsibility for a major renovation to the house in 1988. During their 61 years together, Judie was a faithful, honest and loving friend, as well as wife to Tom for 54 years. Tom has lost the best friend in his life. He will be eternally grateful that Judie civilized him, treated him so well despite his shortcomings and devoted her life to caring for their daughter Olivia. During her final years, Judie received excellent care from her several caregivers, Tina Smith, Ovetta and Shaniesa Gill, Nikki Howell, Nanettee Cansceco and Eden Wildemichael. Oakland Kaiser Permanente staff, especially nurse Dee Dee Bellong, provided wonderful in-home hospice care during the final weeks of her life. Judie was beloved by Tom’s entire family. She was close to Dave Sinclair, her brother-in-law, and Warren Jorgensen, both Willits classmates. She was particularly grateful for her enduring lifelong friendship with LeAnna Spence, a classmate from Willits. In addition Judie cherished her close friendship with Tom’s cousin James Curtiss and her sister-in-law Joan’s friend Peggy Cash. articles.text: Editor: It is astonishing to see the number of Piedmont Unified School District administration and teacher resignations and retirements this school year. With this, a heightened level of animosity is brewing within a growing contingency of Piedmont families towards PUSD. Piedmont parents continue to struggle to ensure their child’s academic needs are met while simultaneously protecting their mental health. During the past two years, the leadership of Randall Booker and Cheryl Wozniak turned their backs on the students and allowed the erosion of PUSD. Students were not the focus of their concerns. Their main concern was the goal of fulfilling DEI initiatives. It is unsettling that PUSD leadership instructed teachers to devote energy to social initiatives rather than utilize the time to help children academically; while failing to earmark additional funds to the Wellness Center to help struggling students. Although DEI is a needed element, it is essential that the PUSD leadership realign its current focus on the needs of the students: academics and mental health. Along with many PUSD families, I maintain hope that the school board will retain a new Superintendent whose sole focus is the educational and mental welfare of students rather than politicized agendas. Ask yourself: “how many more Piedmont families must send their children to local private schools before PUSD leadership wakes up and realizes that there is a major problem within the district?”

With this, a heightened level of animosity is brewing within a growing contingency of Piedmont families towards PUSD. Piedmont parents continue to struggle to ensure their child’s academic needs are met while simultaneously protecting their mental health. During the past two years, the leadership of Randall Booker and Cheryl Wozniak turned their backs on the students and allowed the erosion of PUSD. Students were not the focus of their concerns. Their main concern was the goal of fulfilling DEI initiatives. It is unsettling that PUSD leadership instructed teachers to devote energy to social initiatives rather than utilize the time to help children academically; while failing to earmark additional funds to the Wellness Center to help struggling students. Although DEI is a needed element, it is essential that the PUSD leadership realign its current focus on the needs of the students: academics and mental health. Along with many PUSD families, I maintain hope that the school board will retain a new Superintendent whose sole focus is the educational and mental welfare of students rather than politicized agendas. Of the one hundred, 17 will later become Scout leaders and will provide leadership to thousands of additional Scouts. Only two of the one hundred will reach the rank of Eagle, the highest honor for uniformed Scouts. On May 22, five members of Piedmont’s Troop 1 were celebrated at a National Court of Honor. With paper plates made just for the event, you know it’s a pretty big deal. The ceremony started with the Troop 1 Committee chair, the legendary John Stewart, a longtime former Troop 1 Scoutmaster, convening the event. Senior patrol leader Liam Campbell, the master of ceremony, introduced the Four Winds, a Troop 1 tradition. The winds are two of four Scouts who discuss the importance of the Scout Law. The winds were followed by the Path to Eagle, where Scouts explained the significance of each rank leading up to Eagle. Rank requirements were discussed along with other rank qualifications. Next up was one of my personal favorite parts: the remarks by Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill. I loved hearing him talk about the Eagle Scouts. After the “main event” of the ceremonial presentation of the Eagle medals came a very special Troop 1 tradition. All the patches and merit badges New Eagle Scouts Aaron Drumm (left) Fisher Gibbs, Nicholas Kho, Haik Kibarian, and Theodore Markopoulos. earned by the Eagle Scouts are framed and presented to the honorees as a keepsake. The Eagle Scouts then delivered their own “Eagle remarks,” an opportunity for them to thank everyone who helped on their journey as well as share some stories from their trail to Eagle. The Eagle remarks are among the highlights of the Court of Honor. Their stories and experiences of becoming Eagle really touched me and inspired me to work towards the goal of Eagle. Lastly, an enormous congratulations to the new Eagle Scouts: Aaron Drumm, Fisher Gibbs, Haik Kibarian. Nicholas Koh, Theodore Markopoulos, and their families.
